questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The price of Taiwan, the history, how accessible it is as a foreigner, the gorgeous nature, tasty food as well as it's interesting political landscape

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: We were assigned a student buddy, some were really helpful, others not so much, but it was nice to have someone to direct the questions to. other than that, the international office at NTU was very helpful, all be it, a little slow.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Student buddy, orientation, a few helpful emails regarding course signup, and for a select few (maybe half) access to the dormitories.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
The different share houses are quite cozy and people are generally friendly. One can also use Facebook, or join the What'sApp groups for exchange students in Taipei. The very best option is
591.tw
, that is their Boligportalen, you do need a translator for that, since it is all in Mandarin.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
One can easily live some way off campus, the problem transport is very easy, and if you live in Taipei City, and not New Taipei, then biking is also very easy! Their way of biking does take a few days to get used to.
Since about half of the exchange students are living on campus, or very close to, then most things are happening in that are, apart from night clubs and so on. Expect to bike home or grab an Uber since the trains and buses stops running at midnight.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Just apply for all available dormitory options. Especially the ones in Taipei City. They are quite good, and it is very nice to have the option. I wish NTU offered more spots at the dorms for exchange students, since the positions are only made available a month or two before the start of the semester.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
It feels very bureaucratic, which it is, but as long as you have the correct documents, you are fine. I would recommend getting the health exam done at NTU and not in DK, since it is MUCH cheaper, and very fast. Be ready to spend quite a few hours doing it though, but definitely worth it for saving a couple thousand DKK.
Bring all your papers to Taiwan, and take photos of
them.They
are needed.
Also, on the day you arrive, go get a TW phone number, if you bring the document, that states you are accepted into NTU you can get a student discount. The reason you should go get a TW phone number is because it later appears as a requirement from NTU, and you can only get one phone plan, per visa entry to TW, so just get the longest plan, that fits within your visa period.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
The online preregistration is super easy. When in TW for the final registration: You get a designated time to appear at the academic office to stand in line. You are probably not gonna get in at that time, but better safe than sorry. You are then slowly moving through having people check that you have all your papers. In the end you get your student card and you are fully registered. You need to have done your health check and have a phone number before then. They need you to fill out an online form with emergency contascts that are IN Taiwan! Go to 7/11 for all your printing needs. It is super easy and quite cheap.

Regarding the class registration: There are 3 rounds, the two first rounds of preregistration, where you can pick all the courses you want and then put them in a prioritized list. If you get number 1 on your list it then blocks that time period of your schedule for all other classes you apply for, so you need to be a little tactical about it. After the first round of preregistration you get told which classes you got into, you can then choose to drop some of them and/or repeat the process to try and add more courses. I recommend signing up to any and all you find interesting since the third period is a little stressful.
In the third period you can show up to the first class in the first week, or send an email to the professor, to hopefully get a registration code so you can sign up for the class. This also extends into the second week of the semester, so if you didn't get enough credits the first week fear not. During these two weeks one can also just as well drop courses that seem to intensive or that aren't to your liking. Note that one can also sign up for Badminton, volleyball lessons and so on, as credits. It is in Mandarin, but is definitely feasible as a fun and cheap activity that fosters meeting local students outside the very competitive academic subjects.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There was a short guide online, otherwise, one can always ask one's student buddy or send an email to the office of international affairs.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was very successfull, I registered for some classes I ended up disliking, so I dropped them in the first and second week, which meant I was under the 30 ECTS for a few days until I recieved some codes for some other classes.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Sign up for as many classes as possible. Check NTU rating for some of the courses, not all are available.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Not all professors are speaking amazing english, but some are incredibly good. Some courses are VERY demanding. Others are very much not so.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
Some were quite difficult, partly because I picked courses outside of my subject of maths, and partly because they just teach in a different way in some courses.
I think the level of the courses I took was in general quite at my level.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Some courses really try to be very interactive, but some of the local students are quite shy.
In most courses there's given points for everything, from attendance and participation to big assignments or presentations.
Some felt very much like studying at UCPH, others very much not so.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Combinatorics (I)
General Chinese Beginners I
Programming Language: Functional Programming
International Companions for Learning
Algorithms Design and Analysis
Machine Learning (4 credits)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Studying Chinese/Mandarin is incredibly fun and interesting. The teachers are very good and one can actually learn quite a lot in one semester.
The functional programming course wasn't to intensive, while being really fun and interesting.
The ICL program is so fun! You are having a weekly hour online with some local kids, where you are sharing about your local country, while they, hopefully, share about Taiwan and themself. A part of the program is a free trip to your school as well as neighboring schools in the area.
I'd also recommend taking either an intensive course which allows for less study hours the rest of the semester or a physical course since they seem very fun and interesting. I did neither.
Do not take the python courses if you have any experience programming, unless there's no attendance. Otherwise, you'll be bored out of your mind.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
Not much, maybe how much I used the public transportation? But it isn't very expensive. The bikes are free the first half hour, and afterwards costing 2,2 DKK per half hour, and the metro in Taipei costs between 4,4-5,5 DKK per trip. More if you are travelling further outside Taipei.
Maybe the most unexpected expense was getting a mattress, pillow and duvet/blanket. Just go to IKEA.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Alcohol is a little more expensive than I expected. Beer can often be the same price as in Denmark. Out in the night life you can sometimes get very good happy hour deals. Food is so very inexpensive.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I did Tai Chi for a while which was very cool. In general the clubs are very good! Some are only for Mandarin speakers, but there is a big club fair where you can go around and ask questions

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: So many! There's a bunch of cultural clubs and athletic clubs as well as international clubs for Europe and so on. There aren't a bunch of activities for the whole school, like KU Festival, but there are some smaller ones, arranged by the clubs. The clubs that demand more talking, and doesn't have a clear international focus are probably only in Mandarin.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Go hike. It is gorgeous and very accessible. If you are going on more demanding hikes, less traveled ones, or in bad weather, then make sure to prepare for this with a flashlight, food, rain protection and so on. Nature can actually be scary in Taiwan.
Also just travel around Taiwan, the public transport system is very good, especially in the west, where the high speed rail allows one to get from the south to the north in just 1,5H. Alishan is beautiful, Tainan is so cool and friendly. The east is very interesting. The Hualien night market is great! A lot of indigenous food as well.
Also just meet with as many other students as possible. People are so nice and just want to do stuff with other cool people.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
If it's a Taiwanese holiday I would either stay in Taipei, go abroad or plan well in advance since a lot of Taiwanese are traveling in Taiwan during these holidays.
Otherwise, explore Taipei, go have a nice dinner with friends, go hike, go to another city in Taiwan, get a permit for Jade Mountain/Yushan, go out singing karaoke, enjoy the skyline with Taipei 101. Go do a tea ceremony/do Kung Fu style tea.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
It isn't terribly difficult. The most difficult part is their bike lines which aren't one-way and most are a part of the sidewalks with people walking on them or you end up biking on the road.
In general Taiwanese are very friendly and helpful.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join ICL, through that you get a partner. Try and talk them up in class, they probably really want to talk to you but are too shy. Join a club.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Nothing I can recall. Maybe, the lack of trash cans or their huge focus on performing well in their studies.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
They are very friendly and nice. Especially, if you are outside Taipei. In the capital people mostly mind their own business.
I really enjoy the communal eating.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Participate and do a bunch of activities with the other exchange students in the beginning.
Pick your courses wisely depending on the amount of work you are willing to do. Some courses are very demanding and require a lot of work. Especially around the time of midterms or finals.
Taiwan is amazing!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
NTU is mostly at the one campus, so if off campus you'd be advised to not live to far away from campus.
You do not need to travel or have big plans every weekend. It seems like every one else does, but that isn't necessarily true. Staying in Taipei and living life there is also really valuable. Become a local and find the most amazing local spots!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
Experiencing a very different culture, the breathtaking views and mouthwatering food.
Getting to meet lovely people from all over the world and making some very good friends through this.
Being able to emerge myself and live in a different country for half a year.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
Not having any close friends to lean on when the new friendships are still blooming.
Being able to do all the plans and activities in just a semester.
Balancing school, experiences and friends.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: If you pick NTU, you will not regret it. It's a undiscovered pearl!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
